did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s heading includes musical instructions: “For the director of music, with stringed instruments” and “according to the Sheminith.” The phrase “according to the Sheminith” is an ancient musical term, but its precise meaning is uncertain.

Did you know? This verse is structured in parallel: “Do not rebuke me in your anger” corresponds to “and do not discipline me in your wrath.” The psalmist asks that the rebuke and discipline not come from anger.

Did you know? The psalmist describes his condition in two ways: “I am faint” means that he is suffering and oppressed, while “my bones are shaken” means that his body is trembling or weakened. Alongside this description, he pleads, “Heal me.”

Did you know? In this verse, the distress moves from the body to the soul: “My soul is deeply troubled.” The question, “And you, LORD—how long?” expresses the painful expectation of divine intervention.

Did you know? The three requests—“Return,” “Rescue,” and “Save me”—form a sequence of appeals for deliverance. The reason given is “for the sake of your faithful love”—reliance on the LORD’s mercy, not on any merit the psalmist claims.

Did you know? The psalmist presents an argument related to worship: “For there is no remembrance of you in death; in Sheol, who will give you thanks?” This is the speaker’s argument in the psalm, asking to be spared from death so that he can continue to remember and give thanks.

Did you know? The description of weeping in this verse is intentionally vivid and exaggerated: “Every night I soak my bed” and “I drench my couch with my tears.” This emphasizes the intensity of the suffering and its continuation throughout the night.

Did you know? “My eye grows weak because of grief” describes the eye becoming weakened or dim, while the rest of the verse connects the psalmist’s distress with “all my enemies.” Here too, the description combines physical impairment with pressure from his enemies.

Did you know? The tone of the psalm changes sharply in this verse: after describing his suffering, the psalmist commands “all you workers of evil” to depart from him and declares confidently, “For the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping.”

Did you know? The repetition of the root meaning “hear”—“the LORD has heard” and “he will accept my prayer”—strengthens the psalmist’s confidence that his prayer has not gone unanswered but has been received by the LORD.

Did you know? The psalm ends with a threefold repetition emphasizing the enemies’ fate: “They will be ashamed,” “they will be terrified,” and “they will turn back.” The word “suddenly” adds a sense of abrupt and rapid retreat.
